drapeaux.note: Original language: French (Bastiat, 1850, Introduction). Published English translations exist but word the sentence differently (the FEE edition at fee.org reverses the order, “a good and a bad economist”); the faithful translation of the French is kept. Pamphlet titles vary between editions (“What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen,” “That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen”); the first is used throughout.
The Bastiat quotation in the body is the same translation as citation/text.

titre: Bastiat and the Broken Window: Why Destruction Enriches No One
accroche: A child breaks a window, the glazier pockets six francs. In 1850, an economist shows why this reasoning is a trap.
contenu_vulgarise:
A glazier repairs a broken pane and pockets six francs. The man who had to pay for the repair consoles himself with a widespread line of reasoning: at least it gives someone work. In 1850, the French economist Frédéric Bastiat chose this ordinary scene to open his pamphlet *Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas* (*What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen*), published the year of his death, which came on December 24, 1850, in Rome.

## What Is Seen, What Is Not Seen

Bastiat stages the unruly son of a bourgeois whom he names Jacques Bonhomme. The kid breaks a pane; the glazier comes to replace it and collects six francs. The onlookers who witness the scene draw a satisfied conclusion: the broken window has put money into circulation, so it has served industry. That is **what is seen**: a glazier paid, an activity stimulated. What the onlookers do not see is what Jacques Bonhomme would have done with those six francs had the window remained intact: he might have given them to his shoemaker, for a pair of new shoes. The shoemaker received nothing, and his missed sale is not seen, because it never took place. Jacques Bonhomme, for his part, has lost a window and a pair of shoes, for the price of a window alone: society as a whole has not gained a glazier, it has merely lost a pair of shoes. Bastiat states the rule from his introduction: “The whole difference between a bad Economist and a good one is this: the one sticks to the visible effect; the other takes into account both the effect that is seen and those that must be foreseen.”

## An Error That Does Not Stop at Windows

Bastiat is aiming at a precise target: the defenders of tariffs and of major public works undertaken to “put people to work,” who only ever count the jobs created before their eyes, never those that would have existed elsewhere had the money followed its natural course. The reasoning turns up intact nearly two centuries later, each time a catastrophe is presented as an opportunity for recovery: an earthquake that puts masons to work, a storm that keeps sawmills running. In each case, the calculation stops at the check that is seen being cashed and ignores the checks that will never be signed, because the money has already been used once, elsewhere, to repair rather than to build. Bastiat does not claim that the repair expense is useless: he says that it is not a net gain, only a replacement, and that confusing the two amounts to mistaking a column of expenditures for a creation of wealth.

carte.punch: A child breaks a window. The glazier earns six francs. Why is that a problem?
carte.idee: In 1850, Bastiat shows that the money paid to the glazier is not a gain: it is money that Jacques Bonhomme, the customer, could not spend elsewhere, at his shoemaker's, for example. Destruction does not create wealth, it merely moves it, for the worse.

quiz.question: Why does the onlookers' reasoning, in the parable of the broken window, mislead about the real economic effect of the repair?
choix: Because a broken window always costs more to repair than to build in the first place
Because the glazier immediately redistributes his earnings to the other shopkeepers in the neighborhood
Because they do not count the expense that Jacques Bonhomme could not make elsewhere, at his shoemaker's
Because Jacques Bonhomme would have spent those six francs sooner or later anyway
quiz.explication: The onlookers see only the glazier's visible gain. They do not see the sale of shoes that did not take place: Jacques Bonhomme has lost a window and shoes for the price of a window, and society has gained no net glazier.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When and where does Bastiat die, the very year the pamphlet containing the broken window was published?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The body of the text specifies that Bastiat dies on December 24, 1850, in Rome, the very year of publication of the pamphlet containing the parable of the broken window.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the Bastiat quotation reproduced in the entry, what does a bad economist do compared with a good one?
choix: He systematically foresees all the indirect effects of an expenditure
He refuses to distinguish between public and private spending
He sticks to the visible effect, without taking into account the effects that must be foreseen
He considers that all spending, visible or not, enriches society
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bastiat states the rule in his introduction: the bad economist counts only the visible effect, the good one also takes into account the effects that must be foreseen.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, to what contemporary reasoning does the broken-window error still apply, nearly two centuries later?
choix: Justifying a tax increase by the need to fund education
Explaining why wages rise faster than prices
Demonstrating that international trade always benefits both countries
Presenting an earthquake or a storm as an opportunity for economic recovery
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry cites the example of an earthquake that puts masons to work, or of a storm that keeps sawmills running, as a modern revival of the same reasoning.
